title: Ads, A/B Tests, and the Statistical Reality
subtitle: Why your day-2 'winner' is almost always noise

audioChapters.label: Mental model: minimum sample size > 'we have a winner'

blocks.md:
Day 2 of an A/B test. Variant B is showing a 14% lift in click-through rate. Your boss messages the team channel: 'B is the winner — let's roll out!' Twelve people react with thumbs-ups. Nobody asks how many impressions B has had.

If you have ever shipped this scene, you have spent money to learn that random variance feels exactly like a real result. The whole point of statistical thinking in marketing is to refuse the feeling. The cost of the refusal is small. The cost of skipping it is the entire reason your last six 'winning' campaigns underperformed at scale.

blocks.alt: Two charts side by side. Left: 'Day 2, n=1,200' shows variant B at 14% lift, but with a huge confidence interval that crosses zero. Right: 'Day 7, n=4,700' shows variant B at 3% lift, with a tighter confidence interval that just barely excludes zero.
blocks.caption: Same campaign, different sample sizes. The day-2 'win' shrank to a mild 3% lift once the data caught up.

blocks.title: Mental model: sample size is the unit, not days
blocks.md:
Marketing teams measure experiments in *days* because the dashboard shows days. Statistics measures experiments in *sample size*. They are not the same.

- A 7-day test on a low-traffic campaign can have less data than a 1-day test on a high-traffic one.
- A 'big' lift (14%) on a small sample (1,200) tells you almost nothing.
- A 'small' lift (3%) on a large sample (4,700) can be a real, durable signal.

The rule: **before you launch, compute the minimum sample size you need. Until you hit it, you have no conclusion.** This is the no-conclusion-yet rule. It saves more money than any AI tool ever will.

blocks.caption: Watch a confidence interval shrink in real time as sample size grows. Day 2 is theatre; day 7 starts to talk.

hi-IN.title: Founder ne day 2 mein 'winner' declare kar diya
hi-IN.md:
Bengaluru SaaS, last March. Founder ne A/B test launch kara — naya CTA vs purana. Day 2, naye CTA mein 18% lift. Founder ne Slack pe announce kara: "NEW CTA WINS. ROLLING OUT."

Day 14 — full rollout ke baad — actual conversion *down 4%*. Founder confused. Performance marketer ne dekha — day 2 wala sample tha 800 impressions per variant. Statistical noise band of ±22%. 18% lift was inside the noise.

Founder bola, "data ne galat bola." Bhai, data ne kuch nahi bola. Tu ne sample size dekha hi nahi.

en.title: Day 2 winner, day 14 loser
en.md: A Bengaluru SaaS declared a CTA winner on day 2 with an 18% lift on 800 impressions per variant. The noise band on that sample was ±22%. The 'lift' was inside the noise. Two weeks after rolling out, conversions were *down* 4%. The founder said 'the data lied'. The data said nothing. The sample size was the part that hadn't shown up yet.

blocks.md:
The no-conclusion-yet rule is two sentences:

1. Before launch, compute the minimum sample size needed to detect the *minimum lift you'd act on*, with 80% statistical power and 95% confidence.
2. Until you hit that sample size, the answer to 'who's winning?' is 'no conclusion yet'. Not 'A is leading'. Not 'B looks promising'. *No conclusion yet.*

The math is not optional, but it is also not hard. For a baseline conversion rate of 4% and a minimum detectable lift of 5%, you need roughly **4,700 impressions per variant** to declare a winner with 95% confidence and 80% power. Higher base rates need fewer impressions; smaller lifts need more.

A real number: a Pune D2C wellness brand running Meta ads at 800 impressions per variant per day needs *six days minimum* before any A/B test result is honest. Anything shorter is the team performing rigour without doing it. The dashboard does not tell you this; you have to write it down before launching.

blocks.alt: A horizontal bar showing sample size needed for different minimum detectable lift sizes. 1% lift needs 117,000 impressions. 5% lift needs 4,700. 10% lift needs 1,200. 20% lift needs 300.
blocks.caption: The smaller the lift you want to detect, the bigger the sample you need. Most marketers underestimate this by 5-10x.

blocks.title: Translation: 'Let's A/B test the new ad' → an honest experiment plan

steps.label: Step 1 — Decide what would matter
steps.body: Ask: 'What lift would change our decision?' If a 1% lift wouldn't change anything, don't run a test that needs 100k+ impressions to detect it. Pick the lift you'd act on; usually 5-10%.

steps.label: Step 2 — Compute the sample size
steps.body: For your baseline rate and minimum detectable lift, get the per-variant sample size. Free calculators do this in 30 seconds. Write the number down where the team can see it.

steps.label: Step 3 — Estimate test duration honestly
steps.body: Sample size needed / daily impressions per variant = honest minimum days. If that exceeds your patience, either pick a bigger lift to detect, or run the test on a higher-traffic asset.

steps.label: Step 4 — Pre-register the kill criteria
steps.body: Write down: 'We will not declare a winner before day X. If by day X the lift is < 3%, we'll continue running A.' This is the no-conclusion-yet rule, on paper, before launch.

steps.label: Step 5 — On the date, look at the data and act
steps.body: Not before. Not after seeing day-2 numbers. The point of pre-registration is to bind your future self.

blocks.prompt: Your campaign delivers 600 impressions per variant per day. You compute that to detect a 5% lift, you need 4,700 per variant. Your boss wants a winner declared by Friday (4 days from launch). The honest answer is:

choices.label: Tell the boss: minimum honest test is ~8 days; declaring on Friday is theatre. Either extend the timeline or pick a bigger lift threshold (10%, ~1,200 impressions).
choices.explain: Right. The no-conclusion-yet rule. Honest math, presented as options, lets the boss choose without lying about what's possible.

choices.label: Run anyway and declare the leading variant on Friday.
choices.explain: This is the failure mode the rule was designed to prevent.

choices.label: Use AI to estimate what the result *would* be at full sample size.
choices.explain: Tool-substitution for math doesn't work; the AI's prediction inherits the same noise.

choices.label: Stop running A/B tests; they're too slow.
choices.explain: Throwing out the rigour throws out the only mechanism that distinguishes lift from noise.

hi-IN.title: Cricket scoreboard ka analogy
hi-IN.md:
T20 match. India ne 4 overs mein 60 run banaye. Commentator bola, "India is on track for 360." Tu hassi.

Kyun? Kyunki 4 overs ka data full match predict nahi karta. Variance bahut zyada hai shuru mein.

A/B test bhi waisa hi hai. Day 2 ka data full campaign nahi predict karta. Tu cricket mein commentator par hass-ta hai. A/B test mein khud ban-ta hai.

en.title: The 4-over projection
en.md: When a cricket commentator says 'on track for 360' after 4 overs, you laugh. Early data has huge variance; the projection is meaningless. A/B tests work the same way. Day 2 'projections' have the same problem; the only difference is that nobody laughs at marketing dashboards.

blocks.md:
The second move is a habit of seeing. Every time you look at a 'lift' number, ask: *what's the noise band?* If the lift is inside the noise band, the result is statistically indistinguishable from chance — even if the dashboard makes it look heroic.

The rough heuristic that gets you 80% of the way there:

- For a CTR baseline around 2-5%, the 95% noise band at sample size N is roughly ±2 × √(p(1-p)/N) × 100%.
- At N=1,000, baseline 4%: noise band ±1.2 percentage points, or roughly ±30% of the base rate.
- At N=5,000, same baseline: noise band ±0.55pp, roughly ±14%.
- At N=20,000: noise band ±0.27pp, roughly ±7%.

So: at 1,000 impressions, anything under a 30% lift is noise. At 5,000, anything under 14%. At 20,000, anything under 7%. The 14% lift on 1,200 impressions that started this lesson? Inside the noise band. The team that high-fived was applauding randomness.

blocks.alt: Three rows of dots representing campaign results at different sample sizes (n=1k, n=5k, n=20k). Each row shows variant A and variant B with shaded noise bands. At n=1k the bands fully overlap; at n=20k they barely touch.
blocks.caption: Same hypothetical lift, three sample sizes. The 'winning' signal only stops being noise once the bands stop overlapping.

coach.name: Growth-Lead Gauri
coach.role: D2C veteran, has buried six campaigns that 'won' on noise

intro: Statistical reality time. I'll throw five A/B test situations at you.
Tell me: is this a **real lift**, **inside noise**, or **need more data** (sample isn't yet enough to call it)?
These are real numbers from real campaigns. Most teams get them wrong — the bias is always toward declaring winners. Resist it.

scenarios.situation: Day 2. Variant B shows +14% CTR over A. n = 1,200 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=1,200 the noise band is roughly ±28% of the base rate. A 14% lift sits comfortably inside. Looks dramatic; isn't real.

scenarios.situation: Day 8. Variant B shows +6% CTR over A. n = 22,000 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=22k the noise band is roughly ±7%. A 6% lift is just outside it — borderline real, and worth a confirmation run, but it's a defensible call.

scenarios.situation: Day 4. Variant B shows +8% CTR over A. n = 3,500 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=3,500 noise is ±17%. The 8% sits inside the band. You'd need closer to n=8,000 to call it. Wait, don't kill — keep running.

scenarios.situation: Day 14. Variant B shows +35% CTR over A. n = 800 per variant. (Low-volume B2B campaign.)
scenarios.explain: Day count is irrelevant; sample size is the unit. At n=800 the noise band is enormous (~35%). A 35% lift is right at the edge. Could be real, but the test cannot honestly distinguish lift from noise at this sample.

scenarios.situation: Day 10. Variant B shows +1% CTR over A. n = 50,000 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=50k the noise band shrinks to ±4-5%. A 1% lift is *not* outside noise either. But this is the type of test where nothing wins — the variants are basically equivalent. Honest answer: keep the simpler one.

scenarios.situation: Day 6. Variant B shows +9% CTR over A. n = 5,200 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=5,200 the noise band is ~14%. 9% is inside it; barely. Borderline — most teams call this 'real' and ship. Honest framing: weak signal, would re-confirm with another 7 days.

blocks.title: The classic trap: declared winner at day 2, still noise
blocks.md:
The trap is structural, not personal. Dashboards show daily numbers; daily numbers feel meaningful; meaningful-feeling numbers get acted on. The cure is a habit, not a tool.

The habit: every time someone says 'B is winning', your reflex sentence is **'how many impressions, and what's the noise band?'** If they can't answer both, the answer to 'is B winning?' is no conclusion yet. Repeat this in three meetings and the team starts saying it for you.

blocks.prompt: Drag these into the right order — pre-registering an honest A/B test.

items.label: Define the minimum lift that would change a decision
items.detail: 1%? 5%? 10%? Pick the smallest delta that would actually move you to ship the variant.

items.label: Compute the sample size needed for that lift
Estimate honest test duration
items.detail: Sample size / daily impressions per variant. If too long, escalate or rescope.

items.label: Write down the no-conclusion-yet rule and kill criteria
items.detail: On paper, before launch. Bind your future self.

items.label: Launch — and ignore daily dashboard volatility
items.detail: Looking at day-2 numbers is fine; *deciding* on them is the failure.

items.label: On the pre-registered date, decide and act
items.detail: Honor what you wrote down before you knew the result.

blocks.hint: Lift you'd act on → sample size → duration → write down the rule → launch → decide on the date.

blocks.instruction:
You're running Meta ads for an Indore-based D2C brand. Baseline CTR is 3.5%. Daily impressions per variant: 1,400. You want to detect a 7% lift. Compute:

1. Approximate sample size needed per variant.
2. Honest minimum test duration in days.
3. A one-paragraph 'pre-registration' note you'd email the team before launch — covering the lift threshold, the duration, and what you'll do if the test ends inconclusive.
blocks.expected:
1. Sample size: For baseline 3.5% and 7% relative lift (i.e. detecting +0.245pp), at 80% power and 95% confidence you need approximately 8,500-9,000 impressions per variant.

2. Honest duration: 9,000 / 1,400 ≈ 6.4 days, so seven full days minimum.

3. Pre-registration note:
'Team, launching the cart-recovery email A/B test tomorrow. Variant A = current control; Variant B = new subject line + opening. We've calculated that detecting a 7% relative lift with 95% confidence and 80% power requires ~9,000 impressions per variant; at our current 1,400/day, that's seven days. We will NOT declare a winner before day 7. If by day 7 the lift is below 7% in either direction, our default is to keep variant A (the simpler one) and treat the test as inconclusive. If between 7-15%, we extend by another 3 days for confirmation. If above 15%, we ship. No mid-test rollouts. — [Your Name]'

blocks.prompt: You're presenting test results to a non-technical founder. Which of these are honest framings? (pick two)

choices.label: 'At our current sample size, we cannot distinguish a 14% lift from chance. Decision deferred to day 8 when we'll have 4,700 impressions per variant.'
choices.explain: Honest, specific, action-bound. This is what an honest framing looks like.

choices.label: 'B has shown a real, durable +6% lift over A across 22,000 impressions per variant; recommending we ship B.'
choices.explain: Specific lift, specific sample, specific recommendation. Defensible.

choices.label: 'B is performing better. We're confident.'
choices.explain: Confidence without sample size or lift band. Marketing astrology.

choices.label: 'Day 2 is showing strong B preference; rolling out tomorrow.'
choices.explain: The exact move the no-conclusion-yet rule was invented to prevent.

hi-IN.title: Naani ka tea-tasting test
hi-IN.md:
Naani chai banati hai do versions. Tu ek sip lekar bolta hai, "second one is better." Naani: "Beta, ek hi sip se kaise pata? Doosri ek bana ke do sip de." Tu repeat karta hai. Ab actually pata chalta hai.

A/B test bhi waisa hi hai. *Ek* sip — ek run — sample. Pattern dekhne ke liye tujhe enough volume chahiye. Naani always knew this. Marketing teams forgot.

en.title: The two-cup tea test
en.md: Your grandmother makes you taste two cups; you can't tell them apart on one sip. So you take three more from each. Now you can. Sample size is the only thing changing. Marketing dashboards forgot this; your grandmother didn't.

points: Sample size is the unit of an A/B test, not days — measuring in days is confusing time with information.
The no-conclusion-yet rule: until you hit the pre-registered minimum sample, the answer to 'who's winning?' is no conclusion yet.
Every 'lift' has a noise band; if the lift is inside the band, the result is indistinguishable from chance.
Pre-registration binds your future self to honest decisions before you know the result; without it, you'll find a story for whatever happened.
If your campaign volume cannot deliver an honest sample within an honest timeframe, either pick a bigger lift to detect, or skip the test entirely.

blocks.prompt: Pick the last A/B test your team called. Looking back: what was the sample size, what was the noise band at that size, and was the declared lift inside or outside it? If inside — what did you spend on the rollout?
